records.name: Jigawa
records.summary:
Jigawa is among the twelve northern Nigerian states whose Sharia penal codes, adopted in the 1999–2002 wave, give religious courts criminal jurisdiction over Muslims. A June 2025 government country-of-origin note confirms Jigawa's code remains in force, criminalising same-sex sexual acts by men (death the maximum) and by women (flogging and up to six months' imprisonment) — coverage the federal code, which reaches only men's acts, does not supply independently.

No trans-specific incident, Hisbah record or court-level study covers Jigawa in this dossier; like the rest of the bloc its enforcement statistics are acknowledged as partial. The finding is the enacted parallel jurisdiction and its statutory reach over women's conduct.

freshness.fact: Criminalisation conclusion unchanged: Jigawa's Sharia penal provisions remain in force, now overlaid by the 2014 federal SSMPA; enforcement via arrests and extortion documented through 2024-25.
2019 USCIRF mapping of Sharia criminal provisions still accurate for Jigawa: no state has repealed its provisions since; federal SSMPA unchanged.
Jigawa is among the 12 northern states whose sharia penal codes criminalise same-sex sexual acts by men and women; death maximum for men, flogging and up to 6 months for women.

records.name: Kaduna
records.summary:
Kaduna carries both layers of criminalisation that define Nigeria's northern bloc. Its 2017 secular Penal Code punishes 'unnatural offences' — covering acts between men and between women — with up to 21 years' imprisonment plus fine; and, per a June 2025 government country-of-origin note, the state's Sharia penal code additionally applies to Muslims through religious courts with criminal jurisdiction, in force since the 1999–2002 wave, with the bloc's capital maximum for men's acts.

No trans-specific incident or documented Hisbah enforcement appears for Kaduna in this dossier, and no court-level study samples it. The finding is the stacked architecture: a long-term secular offence alongside a parallel religious jurisdiction, both current.

freshness.fact: Criminalisation unchanged in Kaduna (Sharia provisions + 2014 SSMPA); recent reporting documents entrapment via social media and extortion ('kito') by enforcement officers.
No repeal since the 2019 report; Kaduna's Sharia penal provisions and the SSMPA remain in force.
Kaduna's 2017 secular Penal Code punishes 'unnatural offences' (sodomy, lesbianism) with up to 21 years plus fine; sharia code additionally applies to Muslims; both current per CPIN.

records.name: Katsina
records.summary:
Katsina is one of the twelve northern Nigerian states that built a parallel Sharia criminal jurisdiction over Muslims in the 1999–2002 wave, documented in an international-rights organisation's chapter on the extension and in a June 2025 government country-of-origin note on the country's hybrid legal system. Its code stands out for reach: the same 2025 note records Katsina as one of only two states whose law carries the death penalty as the maximum for same-sex acts between women as well as men.

No court-case study samples Katsina, no Hisbah operation is documented for it, and no trans-specific incident is on record; the elevated statutory reach over women's conduct is the differentiating fact, with the bloc-wide caveat that enforcement data are partial.

freshness.fact: Current source (Jun 2025): Katsina remains a Sharia-penal-code state with same-sex conduct criminalised; part of the northern twelve.
Sharia in force; death maximum for liwat; Katsina is one of only two states (with Kano) where 'lesbianism' also carries a maximum death penalty.

records.name: Kebbi
records.summary:
Kebbi runs Sharia criminal law as one of the twelve northern states that had adopted it by 2002, with Sharia courts exercising criminal jurisdiction over Muslim defendants in parallel with the federal system (Human Rights Watch, 2004). The federal penal code criminalises same-sex conduct nationwide, and the UK Home Office country note (June 2025) records that these twelve states' Sharia penal codes extend that criminalisation to same-sex acts between women, with a maximum of death for men and flogging or imprisonment for women.

No Kebbi-specific enforcement record against trans people exists; the case-level documentation of Sharia enforcement covers three other bloc states (USCIRF study, 2017). For a Muslim or perceived-Muslim trans visitor who is outed, the practical difference from the rest of the country is jurisdictional: exposure to a Sharia court applying a criminal code that is broader in scope and harsher in penalty than the federal statute alone.

freshness.fact: No repeal in Kebbi since the 2019 mapping; Sharia criminal provisions plus the 2014 SSMPA remain in force.
Kebbi is among the 12 northern sharia-penal-code states criminalising same-sex acts (death maximum for men; flogging/imprisonment for women). No Kebbi-specific source in packet — group coverage only.

records.name: Niger
records.summary:
Niger State operates Sharia criminal law as part of the twelve-state northern bloc adopted by 2002, with Sharia courts holding criminal jurisdiction over Muslim defendants (Human Rights Watch, 2004). The federal anti-discrimination statute criminalises same-sex conduct nationwide; the UK Home Office country note (June 2025) records that the Sharia layer in these states extends criminalisation to acts between women.

No Kebbi-style state-specific enforcement or Hisbah record against trans people is documented for Niger; case-level enforcement records exist for other bloc states. The Sharia system adds a parallel criminal jurisdiction that the federation's southern states do not have, under which an outed Muslim or perceived-Muslim trans visitor faces broader charges and harsher penalties than under federal law alone.

freshness.fact: Current source (Jun 2025): Niger State criminalisation unchanged under Sharia provisions applied since 1999-2000 plus the 2014 SSMPA.
Niger state is within the 12 northern sharia-penal-code states criminalising same-sex acts (death maximum for men); federal/state strands also criminalise; current per CPIN.

records.name: Imo
records.summary:
Imo combines community violence with active state policing against gay people. In April 2018 a crowd in Isiala Mbano stripped two men accused of gay sex, beat them and paraded them through the streets with palm leaves tied around them; a follow-up report records that police took the two men in custody. In February 2025 the state police command announced it had stormed a 'same-sex party' at a hotel in Owerri, arresting eight suspects and charging them under the 2014 anti-homosexuality law, citing its 14-year term — the command's briefing expressly framed the enforcement as covering a 'gay, lesbian, bisexual and/or transgender act'.

The pattern runs across years and across modalities: mob justice met without accountability in 2018, and named, state-command enforcement invoking the criminal law in 2025. For a discovered visitor here, risk comes from neighbours and police alike.

records.name: Edo
records.summary:
In May 2018 in Ekpoma, a community discovered two men having sex; one was lynched to death and the other escaped. The coverage framed the act as an 'abominable' one defying 'the traditional laws and heritage of the land', and no prosecution is recorded: customary moral judgement operating lethally, with complete impunity. For national context, a rights-monitoring report published in January 2025 documented 556 violations against real or perceived LGBT people affecting 850 victims across Nigeria in 2024 — and states these are only a fraction of the true scale.

Edo's finding is the Ekpoma killing itself: where a discovered visitor can face lethal 'community justice' invoked in the name of tradition, answered afterwards by nobody.

records.name: Aceh
records.summary:
Aceh is the only province in this country operating a codified religious criminal law of its own: the Qanun on jinayat (No. 6/2014) criminalises same-sex conduct (liwath, musahaqah) and close proximity (khalwat), with public caning as its signature punishment, applied by Islamic Shariah courts and policed by the Wilayatul Hisbah religious force alongside the secular Satpol PP units. Enforcement is active and widening: in August 2025 a Sharia court — sitting behind closed doors — sentenced two men to 80 strokes each for hugging and kissing, caned in a public park before around 100 spectators, with eight more people caned the same day; up to 100 strokes are available for morality offences generally, and Amnesty International called the practice 'state-sanctioned discrimination and cruelty'.

The Qanun does not name transgender people, but enforcement reaches them: a February 2025 boarding-house round-up detained a waria and a gay student facing up to 100 strokes under the liwath provision, with officials urging landlords to police tenants; in January 2018 police detained twelve transwomen and shaved their heads to teach them 'how to act like real men'. Private consensual conduct that carries no criminal penalty in any other province here can be publicly caned by a court in Aceh.
